title: Steam Deck Adds Avg FPS Display for Thousands of Games, Desktop PC Support Coming Soon
body:
Valve has rolled out a new performance‑tracking feature for the Steam Deck, displaying average frames‑per‑second (FPS) figures and detailed histograms on each game’s store page. The data, gathered from users who opt‑in to share anonymous telemetry, gives prospective buyers a clearer picture of how titles run on the handheld. In parallel, the company is extending the collection framework to desktop PC users, laying the groundwork for a broader performance‑benchmarking ecosystem across the Steam platform.

The addition of FPS metrics arrives at a crucial moment for the Steam Deck, whose popularity has surged since its 2022 launch. Early adopters often relied on community forums, YouTube videos, and third‑party benchmarks to gauge whether a game would be playable on the device’s AMD Zen 2 CPU and RDNA 2 GPU. By integrating average framerate data directly into the storefront, Valve reduces the friction of research and empowers shoppers to make more informed decisions without leaving the platform. The histograms further enrich the information, showing the distribution of frame rates rather than a single average, which helps users understand performance stability and potential dips during intensive scenes.

The telemetry is collected only from players who have explicitly consented to share anonymous performance data, a safeguard that aligns with Valve’s broader privacy commitments. Once a user enables the opt‑in, the client reports metrics such as average FPS, 1‑percent low, and 0.1‑percent low values, along with hardware configuration details. These figures are then aggregated and anonymized before being displayed on the store page. Valve says the system currently covers thousands of titles, ranging from indie releases to major AAA franchises, and it will continue to grow as more users contribute data.

Beyond the Deck, Valve’s move signals an ambition to create a universal performance database for the entire Steam ecosystem. By extending the same data‑gathering pipeline to Windows, Linux, and macOS users, the company could eventually provide cross‑platform FPS benchmarks, helping developers optimize their games for a wider range of hardware. This could also benefit the burgeoning “PC as a service” market, where cloud‑based gaming and subscription models thrive on transparent performance expectations. For developers, access to aggregated real‑world data may inform patch prioritisation and future optimisation efforts, reducing reliance on internal testing rigs that may not reflect the diversity of consumer hardware.

Industry analysts note that Valve’s initiative could reshape how performance is communicated in digital storefronts. Historically, console manufacturers have supplied official performance targets, while PC gaming has remained a patchwork of user‑generated benchmarks. A unified, Valve‑curated dataset could set a new standard, encouraging other platforms—such as Epic Games Store or GOG—to adopt similar transparency measures. Moreover, the inclusion of performance histograms addresses a long‑standing criticism that single‑number FPS values can be misleading, especially for titles with volatile frame‑time profiles.

The rollout is not without challenges. Accurate FPS reporting depends on a sufficiently large and diverse sample of users; early data may be skewed toward enthusiasts with higher‑end Deck configurations or overclocked PCs. Valve will need to ensure statistical robustness and guard against manipulation, such as users artificially inflating scores. Additionally, the privacy‑first approach must remain transparent to maintain user trust, especially as data collection expands to the broader PC audience.

Looking ahead, the integration of real‑time performance analytics could evolve into a more interactive toolset, perhaps allowing users to filter results by hardware specs, resolution, or graphics settings. As Valve refines the system and expands its coverage, gamers can expect a richer, data‑driven shopping experience, while developers gain actionable insights into how their games perform across the fragmented PC landscape. The initiative marks a significant step toward demystifying performance expectations on both handheld and desktop platforms, setting the stage for a more informed and efficient gaming ecosystem.
